items.stem: What is the main purpose of an argumentative composition?
options: To persuade the reader to accept a particular point of view
To present both sides equally without judgement
items.answer: To persuade the reader to accept a particular point of view
items.markingKey: Argumentative = one clear stance throughout.

items.stem: This sentence is discursive: ‘While tourism brings income, it also places pressure on housing and the environment, so its value depends on how it is managed.’ Explain how its stance and tone show this.
items.answer: Discursive: weighs both sides and reaches a qualified view.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying discursive; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: weighs both sides and reaches a qualified view.

items.stem: This sentence is argumentative: ‘Zoos are prisons, and it is time we had the courage to close them.’ Explain how its stance and tone show this.
items.answer: Argumentative: one-sided and persuasive.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying argumentative; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: one-sided and persuasive.

items.stem: Rewrite this one-sided claim as a balanced sentence suitable for a discursive essay. ‘Uniforms are the best way to create equality in schools.’
items.answer: Model (discursive): Supporters say uniforms reduce pressure to wear expensive clothes, but opponents argue that they limit self-expression and can be costly.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for presenting more than one view, measured tone and a discourse marker of contrast. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Rewrite this one-sided claim as a balanced sentence suitable for a discursive essay. ‘Fast fashion is a disaster that should be banned immediately.’
items.answer: Model (discursive): Fast fashion makes clothes affordable for many families; however, critics argue that it creates waste and relies on poorly paid workers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for presenting more than one view, measured tone and a discourse marker of contrast. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: ‘Schools should abolish homework.’ Write an argumentative essay giving your views. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: hook; clear stance; three developed reasons with evidence; counter-argument rebutted; forceful conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (2): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: clear, consistent stance; developed reasons with evidence and examples; rhetorical devices used with control; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; cohesive paragraphing; persuasive conclusion.

items.stem: What is a rhetorical device?
options: A technique of language used to persuade or impress an audience
items.answer: A technique of language used to persuade or impress an audience
items.markingKey: E.g. rhetorical questions, tricolon, antithesis, anaphora.

items.stem: This argument uses example from another place: ‘When Pontevedra in Spain removed most cars from its centre, the streets became busier with pedestrians.’ Explain how convincing this type of evidence is.
items.answer: Example from another place: a real-world precedent suggests the idea can work.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying example from another place; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: a real-world precedent suggests the idea can work.

items.stem: This argument uses statistic: ‘In a survey of 500 students, 68% said they slept less than eight hours on school nights.’ Explain how convincing this type of evidence is.
items.answer: Statistic: precise numbers give weight to the claim.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying statistic; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: precise numbers give weight to the claim.

items.stem: Read ‘Of course, deliveries and disabled access must be protected, and they can be, through permits and timed access.’ from an argumentative essay extract, ‘Ban Cars from the City Centre’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Counter-argument (‘Of course’): conceding practical concerns and offering solutions makes the argument appear reasonable.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (counter-argument); 1 for selecting the key words ‘Of course’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. conceding practical concerns and offering solutions makes the argument appear reasonable.

items.stem: Read ‘Supporters report better attendance, happier teachers and lower running costs.’ from an argumentative essay extract, ‘A Four-Day School Week’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Rule of three (‘better attendance, happier teachers and lower running costs’): three benefits give a sense of weight and completeness to the case.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (rule of three); 1 for selecting the key words ‘better attendance, happier teachers and lower running costs’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. three benefits give a sense of weight and completeness to the case.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from an argumentative essay extract, ‘A Four-Day School Week’: (i) ‘Supporters report better attendance, happier teachers and lower running costs.’ (ii) ‘Imagine waking up on a Friday with no alarm and a whole day to read, rest or help at home.’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Rule of three: three benefits give a sense of weight and completeness to the case. (ii) Imperative: the command invites readers to picture the benefit personally, making the idea appealing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (rule of three; imperative) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: ‘Fast fashion should be banned.’ Write an argumentative essay in which you persuade the reader to agree with you. Use a range of evidence and rhetorical devices. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: rhetorical hook; clear thesis; each paragraph a point + evidence + explanation; devices such as antithesis and tricolon used sparingly; rebuttal; memorable final line.

Indicative content: clear, consistent stance; developed reasons with evidence and examples; rhetorical devices used with control; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; cohesive paragraphing; persuasive conclusion.

items.stem: ‘Cities should ban cars from their centres.’ Write an argumentative essay in which you persuade the reader to agree with you. Use a range of evidence and rhetorical devices. Write about 350–450 words.

items.stem: What is antithesis?
options: Placing contrasting ideas side by side in a balanced structure
Repeating a word at the start of each line
items.answer: Placing contrasting ideas side by side in a balanced structure
items.markingKey: E.g. ‘Exhausted students learn very little. Rested students learn a great deal.’

items.stem: Which discourse marker best introduces the second side of a discursive essay?
items.answer: On the other hand
items.markingKey: It signals a shift to the opposing view.

items.stem: Read a discursive essay extract, ‘Is Social Media Good for Young People?’: ‘Social media is now part of everyday life for most teenagers, and opinions about its effects are sharply divided. On the one hand, it allows young people to stay in touch with friends, find communities that share their interests and discover news and ideas from around the world. For a teenager who feels isolated, an online group can be a lifeline. On the other hand, research has linked heavy use to poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly when users compare themselves with carefully edited images. It is also difficult to judge which information is reliable. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that social media is neither simply good nor simply bad: what matters is how, and how much, it is used.’ Explain how the writer signals a balanced structure.
items.answer: Discourse markers ‘On the one hand’ and ‘On the other hand’ divide the two sides; the conclusion begins ‘Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion’, signalling evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: discourse markers; evaluative conclusion; credit for reference to tone.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Read a discursive essay extract, ‘Is Social Media Good for Young People?’: ‘Social media is now part of everyday life for most teenagers, and opinions about its effects are sharply divided. On the one hand, it allows young people to stay in touch with friends, find communities that share their interests and discover news and ideas from around the world. For a teenager who feels isolated, an online group can be a lifeline. On the other hand, research has linked heavy use to poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly when users compare themselves with carefully edited images. It is also difficult to judge which information is reliable. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that social media is neither simply good nor simply bad: what matters is how, and how much, it is used.’ How could the writer make the evidence more convincing? (b) Read a discursive essay extract, ‘Is Social Media Good for Young People?’: ‘Social media is now part of everyday life for most teenagers, and opinions about its effects are sharply divided. On the one hand, it allows young people to stay in touch with friends, find communities that share their interests and discover news and ideas from around the world. For a teenager who feels isolated, an online group can be a lifeline. On the other hand, research has linked heavy use to poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly when users compare themselves with carefully edited images. It is also difficult to judge which information is reliable. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that social media is neither simply good nor simply bad: what matters is how, and how much, it is used.’ Explain how the writer signals a balanced structure.
items.answer: (a) By naming specific studies, giving figures or examples, and showing how reliable each source is. (b) Discourse markers ‘On the one hand’ and ‘On the other hand’ divide the two sides; the conclusion begins ‘Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion’, signalling evaluation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: specificity; 1 mark: source reliability. (b) 1 mark: discourse markers; 1 mark: evaluative conclusion; a further mark for reference to tone.

items.stem: Plan a discursive essay on a four-day school week. Give two developed points for, two against, and a one-sentence conclusion that weighs them.
items.answer: Model: For – rest, attendance, lower costs; Against – childcare, lost learning, longer days; Conclusion – a qualified judgement explaining which points carry most weight and why.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: two points for with development; two against with development; conclusion that weighs rather than repeats.

items.stem: Write the paragraph of a discursive essay on banning mobile phones in schools that moves from the arguments in favour (concentration, less cyberbullying) to the arguments against (safety, learning tools, independence). Use at least two discourse markers.
items.answer: Model: a topic sentence summarising the case for; a turn with ‘However’/‘On the other hand’; development of one or two arguments against with evidence; a linking sentence that prepares for evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: clear transition; arguments on both sides developed; discourse markers used accurately; measured tone.

items.stem: Plan a discursive essay on tourism in fragile places. Give two developed points for, two against, and a one-sentence conclusion that weighs them.
items.answer: Model: For – income, jobs, cultural exchange; Against – damage, rising rents, overcrowding; Conclusion – a qualified judgement explaining which points carry most weight and why.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: two points for with development; two against with development; conclusion that weighs rather than repeats.

items.stem: Write a discursive essay on school uniforms, considering arguments for and against before reaching a conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: introduction framing the debate on school uniforms; paragraph(s) for (equality, identity, lower peer pressure); paragraph(s) against (cost, self-expression, comfort); evaluation; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: balanced exploration of both sides with evidence; points weighed and evaluated; measured, objective tone; discourse markers for structure; reasoned judgement in the conclusion. For: equality, identity, lower peer pressure. Against: cost, self-expression, comfort.

items.answer: Model approach: introduction framing the debate on banning mobile phones in schools; paragraph(s) for (concentration, less cyberbullying); paragraph(s) against (safety, learning tools, independence); evaluation; reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Read a discursive essay extract, ‘Is Social Media Good for Young People?’: ‘Social media is now part of everyday life for most teenagers, and opinions about its effects are sharply divided. On the one hand, it allows young people to stay in touch with friends, find communities that share their interests and discover news and ideas from around the world. For a teenager who feels isolated, an online group can be a lifeline. On the other hand, research has linked heavy use to poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly when users compare themselves with carefully edited images. It is also difficult to judge which information is reliable. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that social media is neither simply good nor simply bad: what matters is how, and how much, it is used.’ Explain why the conclusion is effective for a discursive essay. (b) Read a discursive essay extract, ‘Is Social Media Good for Young People?’: ‘Social media is now part of everyday life for most teenagers, and opinions about its effects are sharply divided. On the one hand, it allows young people to stay in touch with friends, find communities that share their interests and discover news and ideas from around the world. For a teenager who feels isolated, an online group can be a lifeline. On the other hand, research has linked heavy use to poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, particularly when users compare themselves with carefully edited images. It is also difficult to judge which information is reliable. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that social media is neither simply good nor simply bad: what matters is how, and how much, it is used.’ How could the writer make the evidence more convincing?
items.answer: (a) It rejects both extremes and offers a nuanced judgement (how and how much social media is used), which follows logically from the balanced discussion. (b) By naming specific studies, giving figures or examples, and showing how reliable each source is.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: nuance/qualified judgement; 1 mark: follows from both sides. (b) 1 mark: specificity; 1 mark: source reliability.

items.stem: What is the purpose of a rebuttal?
options: To show why an opposing argument is weak or less important
To agree completely with the opposition
items.answer: To show why an opposing argument is weak or less important
items.markingKey: Rebuttal turns a counter-argument to your advantage.

items.stem: Explain why this conclusion is weak and how it could be improved: ‘So that is why I think homework should be banned. Thank you for reading.’
items.answer: Weakness: merely restates and adds an informal sign-off; no final impact. Model: Homework was meant to extend learning; too often it now replaces sleep, rest and family time. It is time to set less, and to set it better.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness; specific improvement; credit for linking to impact on the reader.

items.stem: Explain why this conclusion is weak and how it could be improved: ‘In conclusion, there are good and bad points.’
items.answer: Weakness: vague; no judgement or weighing. Model: On balance, the benefits of tourism can outweigh its costs – but only if islanders, not cruise companies, decide how many visitors arrive.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the weakness; specific improvement; credit for linking to impact on the reader.

items.stem: Opponents argue: ‘Uniforms stop students expressing themselves.’ Write a paragraph that concedes any valid part of this argument and then rebuts it convincingly.
items.answer: Model: Admittedly, uniforms limit choice of clothing; however, self-expression is not only about clothes – students express themselves through their ideas, work and activities, and uniforms reduce costly peer pressure.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: fair statement of the counter-argument; concession marker; rebuttal with reason or evidence; controlled, persuasive tone.

items.stem: Opponents argue: ‘Tourism creates jobs.’ Write a paragraph that concedes any valid part of this argument and then rebuts it convincingly.
items.answer: Model: Tourism does create jobs, but many are seasonal and low-paid, and profits often go to companies abroad; the benefit depends on how tourism is managed.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: fair statement of the counter-argument; concession marker; rebuttal with reason or evidence; controlled, persuasive tone.

items.stem: ‘Schools should abolish homework.’ Write an argumentative essay. Include at least two counter-arguments, each followed by a rebuttal, and end with a persuasive conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: thesis; strongest reason; counter-argument 1 + rebuttal; second reason; counter-argument 2 + rebuttal; conclusion echoing the hook.

Indicative content: clear, consistent stance; developed reasons with evidence and examples; rhetorical devices used with control; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; cohesive paragraphing; persuasive conclusion. Counter-arguments fairly stated and convincingly rebutted; conclusion memorable.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of a discursive composition?
options: To explore different views on an issue in a balanced way before reaching a reasoned conclusion
To list facts with no conclusion
items.answer: To explore different views on an issue in a balanced way before reaching a reasoned conclusion
items.markingKey: Discursive = balanced exploration.

items.stem: This sentence is discursive: ‘Some argue that zoos protect endangered species; others believe they cause unnecessary suffering.’ Explain how its stance and tone show this.
items.answer: Discursive: presents opposing views neutrally.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying discursive; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: presents opposing views neutrally.

items.stem: For the statement ‘Technology has made us lonelier.’, write two short opening paragraphs: one for an argumentative essay and one for a discursive essay. Then explain the key difference in purpose and stance.
items.answer: Model: the argumentative opening states a clear position forcefully (with a hook); the discursive opening introduces the debate and signals that both sides will be weighed. Difference: persuasion versus balanced exploration.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: clear stance in the argumentative opening; balance signalled in the discursive opening; appropriate tone for each; accurate explanation of the difference.

items.stem: Which type of evidence is used here? ‘My cousin worked twenty hours a week in a shop and her grades suffered.’
items.answer: anecdote
items.markingKey: Anecdote: a personal story adds human interest but is weak as proof.

items.stem: In an argumentative essay extract, ‘A Four-Day School Week’ the writer uses the counter-argument ‘Some will argue’: ‘Some will argue that students would simply lose a day of learning. But longer, better-planned days can cover the same content’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: the objection is raised and rebutted, making the writer seem fair and confident.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Some will argue’. Model point: the objection is raised and rebutted, making the writer seem fair and confident. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Develop this undeveloped claim into a persuasive point with a reason, evidence or example and an explanation. ‘Homework is bad.’
items.answer: Model: Homework set late at night competes with sleep; when students lose sleep, their memory and concentration suffer, so excessive homework can undermine the learning it is meant to support.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for a clear reason, specific evidence or example, explanation of why it matters, and controlled persuasive language. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Read an argumentative essay extract, ‘Ban Cars from the City Centre’. ‘Every morning, the same scene: engines idling, horns blaring, a grey haze hanging over the square. Our city centre has become a car park with shops attached. Air pollution is linked to millions of early deaths worldwide each year, and children, who breathe faster and walk closer to exhaust pipes, are among the most vulnerable. Cities that have pedestrianised their centres have often seen footfall rise rather than fall. Of course, deliveries and disabled access must be protected, and they can be, through permits and timed access. But the principle is clear. Streets should belong to people, not to traffic.’ How does the writer build a persuasive argument for banning cars? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Vivid opening; witty metaphor; statistic and concern for children; evidence from other cities (vague); concession with solutions; short, principled conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Vivid opening; witty metaphor; statistic and concern for children; evidence from other cities (vague); concession with solutions; short, principled conclusion.

items.stem: Read an argumentative essay extract, ‘A Four-Day School Week’. ‘Imagine waking up on a Friday with no alarm and a whole day to read, rest or help at home. A four-day school week is not a fantasy; schools in several countries have trialled it. Supporters report better attendance, happier teachers and lower running costs. Some will argue that students would simply lose a day of learning. But longer, better-planned days can cover the same content, and the fifth day could be used for sport, volunteering or independent projects. Exhausted students learn very little. Rested students learn a great deal. The question is not whether we can afford to change, but whether we can afford not to.’ How does the writer try to persuade the reader to support a four-day school week? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Imperative hook; claim of trials as evidence (though vague); rule of three; counter-argument and rebuttal; contrasting short sentences; antithesis in the conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (reading). Top band (9–12): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (5–8): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–4): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Imperative hook; claim of trials as evidence (though vague); rule of three; counter-argument and rebuttal; contrasting short sentences; antithesis in the conclusion.

items.stem: This argument uses expert opinion: ‘According to a sleep scientist at a national university, teenagers’ body clocks shift later during puberty.’ Explain how convincing this type of evidence is.
items.answer: Expert opinion: authority supports the claim.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying expert opinion; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: authority supports the claim.

items.stem: This argument uses logical reasoning: ‘If students are exhausted, they cannot concentrate; if they cannot concentrate, they cannot learn.’ Explain how convincing this type of evidence is.
items.answer: Logical reasoning: a chain of cause and effect makes the conclusion seem inevitable.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying logical reasoning; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: a chain of cause and effect makes the conclusion seem inevitable.

items.stem: Plan a discursive essay on online learning. Give two developed points for, two against, and a one-sentence conclusion that weighs them.

items.stem: A student ends an argumentative essay with this sentence: ‘So that is why I think homework should be banned. Thank you for reading.’ Explain what makes it an ineffective conclusion.
items.answer: Merely restates and adds an informal sign-off; no final impact.

items.stem: Rewrite this conclusion so that it is persuasive and memorable. ‘In conclusion, also another reason is that zoos are expensive.’
items.answer: Model: Zoos can still play a role, but only as sanctuaries for species that truly need them – anything more is entertainment dressed as conservation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for a clear final judgement, a link to the essay’s main idea and a memorable final sentence; the original was introduces a new point instead of concluding. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Rewrite this conclusion so that it is persuasive and memorable. ‘So that is why I think homework should be banned. Thank you for reading.’
items.answer: Model: Homework was meant to extend learning; too often it now replaces sleep, rest and family time. It is time to set less, and to set it better.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for a clear final judgement, a link to the essay’s main idea and a memorable final sentence; the original was merely restates and adds an informal sign-off; no final impact. items.stem: Which tone is most appropriate for a discursive essay?
items.answer: Measured and objective
items.markingKey: Discursive writing weighs evidence calmly.

items.stem: This sentence is informative: ‘Homework was introduced in many countries in the nineteenth century and is now set in most secondary schools.’ Explain how its stance and tone show this.
items.answer: Informative: presents facts without taking a side.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying informative; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: presents facts without taking a side.

items.stem: Rewrite this one-sided claim as a balanced sentence suitable for a discursive essay. ‘Space exploration is humanity’s greatest achievement and deserves unlimited funding.’
items.answer: Model (discursive): Space programmes have produced useful technologies, yet many argue that the money could address urgent problems on Earth.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for presenting more than one view, measured tone and a discourse marker of contrast. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Read ‘Every morning, the same scene: engines idling, horns blaring, a grey haze hanging over the square.’ (an argumentative essay extract, ‘Ban Cars from the City Centre’). Which language feature does the writer use here?
items.answer: Listing
items.markingKey: Listing: a series of items piled up one after another. Here ‘engines idling, horns blaring, a grey haze’ – the list of images creates a vivid, unpleasant picture to hook the reader.

items.stem: ‘Every morning, the same scene: engines idling, horns blaring, a grey haze hanging over the square.’ (an argumentative essay extract, ‘Ban Cars from the City Centre’). What does the phrase ‘engines idling, horns blaring, a grey haze’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the list of images creates a vivid, unpleasant picture to hook the reader.

items.stem: Read ‘The question is not whether we can afford to change, but whether we can afford not to.’ from an argumentative essay extract, ‘A Four-Day School Week’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Repetition (‘can afford’): the reversed phrase (antithesis) creates a powerful, quotable conclusion that turns the cost argument around.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (repetition); 1 for selecting the key words ‘can afford’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the reversed phrase (antithesis) creates a powerful, quotable conclusion that turns the cost argument around.

items.stem: ‘Every young person should do a year of community service.’ Write an argumentative essay in which you persuade the reader to agree with you. Use a range of evidence and rhetorical devices. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: rhetorical hook; clear thesis; each paragraph a point + evidence + explanation; devices such as antithesis and tricolon used sparingly; rebuttal; memorable final line.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (2): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: clear, consistent stance; developed reasons with evidence and examples; rhetorical devices used with control; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; cohesive paragraphing; persuasive conclusion.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘people, not to traffic’ in this line from an argumentative essay extract, ‘Ban Cars from the City Centre’: ‘Streets should belong to people, not to traffic.’
items.answer: the short, balanced final sentence states the principle memorably.

items.stem: Write the paragraph of a discursive essay on a four-day school week that moves from the arguments in favour (rest, attendance, lower costs) to the arguments against (childcare, lost learning, longer days). Use at least two discourse markers.
items.answer: Model: a topic sentence summarising the case for; a turn with ‘However’/‘On the other hand’; development of one or two arguments against with evidence; a linking sentence that prepares for evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: clear transition; arguments on both sides developed; discourse markers used accurately; measured tone.

items.stem: Write a discursive essay on zoos, considering arguments for and against before reaching a conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: introduction framing the debate on zoos; paragraph(s) for (conservation, education, research); paragraph(s) against (stress, small enclosures, money could protect habitats); evaluation; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: balanced exploration of both sides with evidence; points weighed and evaluated; measured, objective tone; discourse markers for structure; reasoned judgement in the conclusion. For: conservation, education, research. Against: stress, small enclosures, money could protect habitats.

items.stem: A student ends an argumentative essay with this sentence: ‘In conclusion, also another reason is that zoos are expensive.’ Explain what makes it an ineffective conclusion.
items.answer: Introduces a new point instead of concluding.

items.stem: Opponents argue: ‘A four-day week means less learning.’ Write a paragraph that concedes any valid part of this argument and then rebuts it convincingly.
items.answer: Model: It may seem that removing a day reduces learning, but longer, better-structured days can cover the same content, and rested students learn more effectively.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: fair statement of the counter-argument; concession marker; rebuttal with reason or evidence; controlled, persuasive tone.

items.stem: Rewrite this conclusion so that it is persuasive and memorable. ‘In conclusion, there are good and bad points.’
items.answer: Model: On balance, the benefits of tourism can outweigh its costs – but only if islanders, not cruise companies, decide how many visitors arrive.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for a clear final judgement, a link to the essay’s main idea and a memorable final sentence; the original was vague; no judgement or weighing. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.
